source: Somsak Wannasaree, "Banana Orchards" (Khmer translation, 1997), section 4 (varieties grown locally)
text:
This source (a Thai orchard manual translated for Battambang-area use in 1997) describes the same core commercial varieties as the newer MAFF manual, with some added comparative detail useful for choosing between them:

Chek Ambong Mas ("Golden Ambong") is described as the most economically important variety for both domestic sale and export, with a pseudostem 4-8m tall, dark green wax-coated sheaths, and a relatively early bearing time (fruit ready roughly 9 months after planting). Its main weakness is thin skin that bruises and wind-damages easily.

Chek Ambong Khiev ("Green Ambong") has a thicker pseudostem and thicker peel that stays somewhat greenish even when ripe, making it noticeably more resistant to bruising and rough handling than Golden Ambong, at some cost in visual appeal for buyers who expect a fully yellow banana.

Chek Pong Moan ("hen's egg banana") has a thin, non-waxy pseudostem, a small round bunch, and very sweet, high-quality flesh, but is more fragile/perishable than the Ambong types.

Chek Nam Va is noted specifically for drought and wind tolerance and a firmer, less-sweet flesh that holds up well when cooked, making it a common choice both as a snack banana and as a cooking banana; the source also mentions reddish (Nam Va Krahom) and white-fleshed (Nam Va Sor) variants.

Chek Roveak (also called Chek Krouch Deang) is mentioned as a plantain-type cooking banana with a bland, starchy flesh not suited to fresh eating, typically producing a large bunch (cited around 13 hands) and used only after cooking.

Overall takeaway for a farmer choosing a variety: Golden Ambong maximizes market appeal and early income but needs the most careful post-harvest handling; Green Ambong and Nam Va trade some market appeal for sturdier fruit; Pong Moan is a premium-eating but fragile choice; and Roveak/plantain types serve a cooking-banana market rather than the fresh-fruit market.
